title: Snoozer Quinn, the progressive guitarist
summary: Snoozer Quinn strolled tables at Suburban Gardens, later joined Whiteman, drank, was a soloist rather than a band player, and Wiggs recorded him dying.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players

blocks.x: Uh, did you know Snoozer Quinn?

I knew Snoozer very well. Snoozer was a great guitarist. I don't have any pictures of Snoozer. He was a great guitarist, and he had a technique of playing guitar, and he'd be shaking hands with somebody and he'd still be playing his guitar with his fingers like that. Uh-huh. And, uh, he was, he went, uh, after, after he was with us, with, out at, uh, Suburban Gardens. Well, he didn't play with the band. He was strictly a soloist. Uh-huh. And he'd go, he'd go over to different tables and play for people at, at, at tables. Uh-huh. The stroller. Yeah, the stroller. And, uh, then he went with, uh, he went with Whiteman, and it's the same way. He, Whiteman, when Whiteman found somebody at the table, well, that was his child, you know, my, his play toy. And, uh, but Snoozer was a pretty bad drinker. He used to drink a lot. And, uh, but he was still, he was ahead of the game. He was ahead of, he was ahead of what music we were playing. And we appreciated his, his, his virtuosity, I would say. He had a countryside too, didn't he? Huh? He had a country style side too, didn't he? Yeah. He was from Bugalusa. Uh-huh. He was from Bugalusa. And, uh, he also liked to drink too. That was his... You ever hear him play fiddle?
No, I never heard him play fiddle.
I just have heard about that.
Oh, really? Yeah. I mean, that was very country. I never heard him play fiddle.
I understand, you know, a real cornfield.
I never heard him play fiddle.

Well, Snoozer was, I had a lop-shaped head. Yeah, he was, he was, like a miscarriage or something like that. His head was all cock-eyed. Do you remember him? I never saw him. His head was all cock-eyed. He looked, he like, he looked like a misfit. Yeah.
I think it was a Berkeley band. Yeah.

But, uh, he was a very talented musician. Did you play in any bands with him? He was not a good band player. No, he was not a good player. He was a soloist. He wanted to play, he wanted to play the solo all the time himself. So, I mean, you'd let him play and he'd sit down and just listen to him. But, uh, he had, uh, he had a style that was, it was, it was... Please. Please.
It was not even what we were used to listening to. In other words, it was a new style. How would you describe the style? Strictly modernistic. Not modernistic, but I mean progressive.
He was like Sigildia in his time, but in general.
Yeah, exactly. You've heard his records? I've never heard any of his records.
I never did hear any of his records. I never did hear his records.
He was dying, that didn't really set some records. But you know, they both did. He was dying in the hospital.
Yeah, and Wiggs went there and recorded him. Really on his death.
